claims.text: Corrosion protection retention or degradation in pre-exposure Q235 steel is governed by microstructure-controlled formation of the surface oxide scale.
Controlled annealing can refine the grain structure and modify the grain-boundary characteristics of Q235 steel.
Annealing temperature and duration can influence microstructural evolution during high-temperature salt exposure.
Grain size and grain-boundary distribution dictate oxide-scale cohesiveness, porosity, and adherence in Q235 steel.
Under aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C, annealing-induced grain refinement enables a more uniform, coherent, and adherent iron-based oxide layer to form on Q235 steel.
The as-received Q235 steel has a coarse-grained microstructure.
The coarse-grained structure of untreated Q235 promotes rapid iron diffusion at high temperature.
Rapid iron diffusion in untreated Q235 produces thick, porous, and poorly adherent iron-oxide scales.
Porous and poorly adherent oxide scales spall during aggressive salt attack and thereby accelerate corrosion.
Annealed Q235 will show less oxide-scale spallation than non-annealed Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
Annealed Q235 will show lower mass change and lower corrosion rates than non-annealed Q235 during high-temperature salt exposure.
At room temperature, annealed and non-annealed Q235 both form thin oxides that provide limited protection.
Differences in corrosion behavior between annealed and non-annealed Q235 will be minimal at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism is limited to plain carbon steels such as Q235.
Alloy and stainless steels may not follow the proposed mechanism because they inherently form more stable passive films.
A controlled comparison will expose annealed Q235, as-received Q235, and a stainless-steel reference to identical salt environments at room temperature and 700–900 °C.
Mass change, oxide morphology and thickness, oxide phase composition, and spallation can be measured by gravimetry, SEM, XRD, and microscopy.
The absence of statistically significant high-temperature differences in oxide coherence, mass change, and corrosion rate between annealed and non-annealed Q235 would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as pre-exposure Q235, but the intervention refers to annealing 'pre-exposed' Q235 before corrosion testing. Pre-exposed implies prior exposure, whereas pre-exposure implies that exposure has not yet occurred.
